title: Spring Boot Connection Pooling Mechanics
content: Can you explain how connection pooling works in a Spring Boot application connecting to PostgreSQL, and why it is critical for performance?
expected_answer: Connection pooling (defaulting to HikariCP in Spring Boot) maintains a cache of active, physical database TCP connections. Instead of paying the expensive latency cost of establishing a new TCP connection and TLS handshake for every incoming HTTP request, worker threads borrow an existing connection from the pool, execute SQL, and return it. This prevents database server connection exhaustion and drastically lowers response times.

title: JWT Token Verification and Expiration Strategies
content: How does a stateless backend verify a JWT, and how do you handle token revocation if the token is stateless?
expected_answer: A stateless backend verifies a JWT by decoding the Base64 header and payload, computing the cryptographic signature using its secret/public key, and comparing it against the incoming signature. If it matches and the expiration claim (exp) is valid, the request is authenticated without database lookups. For revocation before expiration, industry approaches use short-lived access tokens (10-15 mins) paired with refresh token rotation stored in Redis, or an in-memory token blocklist for invalidated tokens.

title: REST API Idempotency and HTTP Verbs
content: What is idempotency in REST APIs, which HTTP verbs are idempotent, and how do you ensure payment creation endpoints remain safe against duplicate submissions?
expected_answer: An HTTP method is idempotent if executing it multiple identical times produces the exact same server state as a single invocation. GET, PUT, DELETE, and HEAD are idempotent; POST is inherently non-idempotent. To protect non-idempotent payment creation (POST) against client retries, systems utilize an Idempotency-Key header stored in Redis or database unique constraint tables.

title: React Re-Rendering Mechanics and Hook Optimization
content: When does a React component re-render, and how do you prevent unnecessary re-renders in large component trees?
expected_answer: A React component re-renders when its state updates, its parent re-renders, or its consumed Context value changes. Unnecessary re-renders are prevented by structuring state locally, wrapping expensive child components in React.memo, memoizing callback references with useCallback, and caching heavy computations using useMemo.

title: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) Mechanics
content: What is CORS, why does the browser enforce it, and what happens during a preflight OPTIONS request?
expected_answer: CORS is a browser security mechanism enforcing the Same-Origin Policy (SOP). It prevents malicious scripts on one origin from making unauthorized cross-origin requests to another origin without server permission. For non-simple requests (methods like PUT/DELETE or custom headers), the browser sends an automatic preflight OPTIONS request asking the server for Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods, and Allow-Headers before dispatching the real payload.

title: Docker Containerization vs Virtual Machines
content: What is the architectural difference between a Docker container and a traditional Virtual Machine?
expected_answer: A Virtual Machine runs a full guest operating system on top of a hypervisor (Type 1 or 2), virtualizing hardware and requiring gigabytes of RAM and slow boot times. A Docker container shares the host OS kernel and isolates processes using Linux namespaces (PID, net, mount) and cgroups (CPU, memory limits). Containers boot in milliseconds with near-zero virtualization overhead.

title: Relational Foreign Keys and Referential Integrity
content: What is referential integrity in relational databases, and what are the trade-offs of ON DELETE CASCADE versus ON DELETE RESTRICT?
expected_answer: Referential integrity guarantees that foreign key relationships remain valid: a child table cannot reference a non-existent parent row. ON DELETE RESTRICT (or NO ACTION) rejects parent deletion if dependent child rows exist, protecting against accidental data loss. ON DELETE CASCADE automatically deletes all dependent child rows when the parent is deleted, which simplifies cleanup but risks unintended catastrophic data loss in deeply nested relationship graphs.

title: Database Normalization Forms 1NF through 3NF
content: Can you define First, Second, and Third Normal Form (1NF, 2NF, 3NF), and explain when you would intentionally denormalize a table?
expected_answer: 1NF requires atomic values (no repeating groups/arrays) and a primary key. 2NF requires 1NF and that all non-key attributes are fully functionally dependent on the entire composite primary key (no partial dependencies). 3NF requires 2NF and no transitive dependencies (non-key columns must not depend on other non-key columns). Denormalization is intentionally applied in read-heavy analytics or high-traffic reporting to eliminate expensive multi-table joins.

title: Git Branching Strategies and Merge Conflict Resolution
content: Explain the difference between git merge and git rebase, and how you resolve merge conflicts safely.
expected_answer: Git merge combines two branch histories by creating a dedicated 3-way merge commit with two parents, preserving the exact chronological record. Git rebase rewrites project history by taking commits from the feature branch and replaying them on top of the base branch, producing a linear commit history. When conflicts occur, developers manually inspect conflicting lines between HEAD and incoming changes, verify tests pass, and complete the operation.

title: Database B-Tree Indexing and Query Performance
content: How does a B-Tree index accelerate SQL queries, and what is the trade-off of having too many indexes on a table?
expected_answer: A B-Tree index maintains a self-balancing tree structure where leaf nodes contain indexed column values paired with row pointers. Queries with equality or range filters traverse the tree in O(log N) disk page reads instead of an O(N) full table scan. However, every additional index incurs write overhead on INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations because the DBMS must update the table storage pages and every corresponding index structure, causing write amplification and higher storage consumption.

title: Redis Caching Strategies and Thundering Herd Mitigation
content: Explain the Cache-Aside pattern. What is a Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd problem), and how do you prevent it in production?
expected_answer: In Cache-Aside, the application checks cache first; on a miss, it queries the database, writes the result to cache with a TTL, and returns it. A Cache Stampede occurs when a high-traffic key expires, causing hundreds of concurrent requests to experience simultaneous misses and hit the database at once. It is mitigated using distributed mutex locks (SET key lock NX EX) so only one thread recomputes the cache while others wait, or via probabilistic early expiration (XFetch algorithm).

title: Microservices Resilience and Circuit Breakers
content: How does the Circuit Breaker pattern prevent cascading failures in a microservices architecture? Explain Closed, Open, and Half-Open states.
expected_answer: The Circuit Breaker pattern prevents thread pool exhaustion when a downstream dependency fails. In Closed state, requests pass normally; if the error rate exceeds a threshold, it transitions to Open. In Open state, requests fail fast immediately without calling the remote service, invoking a fallback. After a timeout, it transitions to Half-Open, allowing trial requests to test if the service has recovered.

title: Next.js Rendering Strategies: SSR vs SSG vs ISR
content: Explain Server-Side Rendering (SSR), Static Site Generation (SSG), and Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) in Next.js. How does ISR achieve both speed and fresh data?
expected_answer: SSG generates static HTML at build time for instant CDN delivery. SSR generates HTML on every HTTP request on the server, guaranteeing fresh data at the cost of server compute and higher TTFB. ISR combines both: it serves statically cached HTML instantly, and after a configured revalidation time, a background request regenerates the page and updates the CDN cache asynchronously without blocking the user.

content: What is the difference between Liveness, Readiness, and Startup probes in Kubernetes, and what happens when each fails?
expected_answer: Startup probe checks if the application has initialized (prevents killing slow-starting apps). Liveness probe checks if the process is alive; if it fails, the kubelet kills and restarts the container. Readiness probe checks if the pod can accept network traffic; if it fails, the pod is temporarily removed from the Service's endpoint routing without restarting the container.

expected_answer: Multi-stage builds separate the build environment (compilers, build tools, SDKs) from the runtime environment. Artifacts compiled in builder stages are copied into a minimal production base image (Alpine or Distroless). This reduces image size from gigabytes to megabytes, accelerating image pull times, and reduces security vulnerabilities (CVEs) by stripping out compilers and shells.

title: PostgreSQL Transaction Isolation Levels and MVCC
content: Explain Read Committed vs Repeatable Read isolation levels. How does PostgreSQL's Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) prevent dirty reads without locking rows?
expected_answer: In Read Committed, each query within a transaction sees data committed before that query began. In Repeatable Read, the transaction captures a snapshot at its start and sees data committed before the transaction began. PostgreSQL MVCC achieves this without read locks by storing row versions with xmin and xmax transaction IDs; readers only see row versions visible to their active transaction snapshot.

title: PostgreSQL GIN vs B-Tree vs BRIN Indexing
content: When would you choose a GIN index or a BRIN index over a standard B-Tree index in PostgreSQL?
expected_answer: B-Tree is the default for scalar equality and range queries. GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) is chosen for composite multi-value attributes like JSONB documents, arrays, and full-text search where an item contains multiple searchable tokens. BRIN (Block Range Index) is chosen for massive append-only tables where data is naturally ordered on disk (timestamps, serial IDs); it indexes page block min/max values, using kilobytes of RAM instead of gigabytes.

title: Database Query Plan Analysis with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
content: How do you use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify SQL performance bottlenecks? What is the difference between an Index Scan, an Index Only Scan, and a Bitmap Heap Scan?
expected_answer: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and shows estimated cost vs actual execution time, rows, and buffer hits. An Index Scan traverses the index and fetches table heap pages for each row. An Index Only Scan retrieves all needed columns directly from the index without reading table heap pages (if visibility map confirms). A Bitmap Index Scan creates an in-memory bitmap of matching row locations and reads heap pages sequentially.

title: Distributed System Consistency: The CAP Theorem and PACELC
content: Critique the classical CAP theorem. What is the PACELC theorem, and how does it more accurately describe modern distributed databases?
expected_answer: The CAP theorem states that under a network Partition (P), a distributed system must choose between Consistency (C) and Availability (A). However, network partitions are rare; PACELC extends CAP by stating: If there is a Partition (P), how does the system trade off Availability (A) and Consistency (C)? Else (E), when the system is running normally, how does it trade off Latency (L) and Consistency (C)? For example, MongoDB and DynamoDB default to PA/EL (prioritizing latency under normal operation).

title: Distributed Transactions: 2PC vs Saga Pattern
content: Compare Two-Phase Commit (2PC) with the Saga Pattern for managing transactions across distributed microservices. How do Choreography and Orchestration Sagas differ?
expected_answer: Two-Phase Commit (2PC) guarantees atomic consistency via a coordinator using prepare and commit phases, but it suffers from blocking locks, high latency, and coordinator single-point-of-failure. The Saga Pattern decomposes transactions into a series of local transactions coordinated through asynchronous messaging; if a step fails, compensating transactions are executed to undo changes. Choreography relies on event-driven peer-to-peer pub/sub; Orchestration uses a centralized orchestrator directing each service.

title: Kafka Partitioning, Consumer Groups, and Exactly-Once Semantics
content: How does Kafka achieve horizontal scalability through partitioning? How do consumer groups work, and how does Kafka achieve Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS)?
expected_answer: Kafka scales horizontally by dividing topics into partitions across broker nodes. Partitions represent the unit of parallelism, guaranteeing strict order only per partition key. A consumer group assigns each partition to exactly one consumer instance. Exactly-Once Semantics (EOS) is achieved using idempotent producers (sequence numbers and producer IDs preventing duplicates) and transactional coordinators that atomically commit message writes and consumer offset commits together.

title: Full-Stack Security: Mitigating XSS, CSRF, and Token Hijacking
content: Design an end-to-end authentication and session architecture resilient against XSS, CSRF, and token theft. Where should tokens be stored, and how should refresh tokens be handled?
expected_answer: Store short-lived access tokens (10-15 mins) in memory or in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict cookie to prevent theft via JavaScript XSS. Store refresh tokens in HttpOnly cookies with path restriction. Implement Refresh Token Rotation (RTR): issuing a new refresh token on every exchange and invalidating the entire family if an already-used token is reused (indicating theft). Combine with strict Content Security Policy (CSP) and anti-CSRF headers for state-changing requests.

title: Kubernetes Production Zero-Downtime Deployments and Ingress
content: Design a zero-downtime deployment pipeline in Kubernetes. How do you handle database schema migrations alongside rolling deployments without breaking live users?
expected_answer: Zero-downtime rolling deployments require readiness probes so new pods only receive traffic once healthy, and preStop hooks with graceful termination signals (SIGTERM) allowing in-flight connections to complete. Database schema migrations must follow the Expand and Contract pattern (Parallel Run): 1) Expand database (add new nullable column/table), 2) Deploy new code writing to both old and new columns, 3) Backfill historical data, 4) Deploy code reading only new column, 5) Contract database (drop old column).

criteria: Mentions preStop hooks and terminationGracePeriodSeconds for in-flight requests
Explains readiness probes preventing premature traffic routing
Explains Expand and Contract (Parallel Run) migration pattern
rubric.high_score_criteria: Details canary rollouts with service mesh (Istio/Envoy) traffic splitting, connection draining, and backward-compatible serialization.
rubric.low_score_criteria: Recommends running breaking schema migrations directly inside pod startup scripts during rolling updates.

scoring.5: Exemplary production design covering graceful pod shutdown, traffic draining, and Expand/Contract database migration steps.
scoring.3: Explains rolling updates and readiness probes but vague on database backward compatibility.
scoring.1: Has no strategy for handling database migrations during deployments.

title: PostgreSQL Sharding, Table Partitioning, and Multi-Tenant Isolation
content: Compare declarative table partitioning with horizontal sharding and multi-tenant schema isolation in PostgreSQL. How do you design for a 10 TB multi-tenant SaaS application?
expected_answer: Table partitioning splits a single database instance's tables by range/list/hash for query pruning and fast archival. Multi-tenant schema isolation uses separate PostgreSQL schemas per tenant for security isolation. When data volume and write throughput exceed single-node vertical capacity, horizontal sharding distributes tenants across independent database nodes using hash or tenant-id routing. For 10TB SaaS, a hybrid approach shards tenants across clusters while partitioning large audit/timeseries tables within each tenant shard.

criteria: Distinguishes single-node partitioning from distributed multi-node sharding
Evaluates multi-tenant isolation patterns (shared table with tenant_id, schema per tenant, database per tenant)
Proposes shard key routing and partition pruning

rubric.low_score_criteria: Claims partitioning allows infinite horizontal scaling across separate servers or recommends separate databases for 100,000 tenants.

scoring.3: Explains partitioning and sharding correctly but weak on multi-tenant trade-offs.
scoring.1: Confuses partitioning with sharding.

title: RAG Systems: Vector Search, Context Window Optimization, and Evaluation
content: Explain the architecture of an Advanced RAG pipeline. How does Hybrid Retrieval (Dense + Sparse) with Reciprocal Rank Fusion outperform naive vector search, and how do you quantitatively measure RAG quality?
expected_answer: Naive RAG relies solely on dense vector search, which often misses exact keyword queries (acronyms, code identifiers, part numbers). Advanced RAG uses Hybrid Search combining dense semantic vectors (pgvector) and sparse BM25 full-text search, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) to score candidate chunks. Two-stage re-ranking (Cross-Encoder) filters Top-N candidates down to Top-K to overcome the 'Lost in the Middle' problem. RAG quality is quantitatively measured using the RAG Triad: Faithfulness (zero hallucination against retrieved context), Answer Relevance (answering user query without drift), and Context Precision/Recall.

criteria: Contrasts semantic dense search vs exact sparse keyword BM25 search
Explains Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) formula and rank merging
Mentions Two-Stage Re-ranking overcoming 'Lost in the Middle' phenomenon
Identifies RAG Triad metrics: Faithfulness, Answer Relevance, Context Precision/Recall
rubric.high_score_criteria: Details mathematical RRF formula (1/(k+rank)), chunking strategies with metadata pre-filtering, cross-encoder latency trade-offs, and automated LLM-as-a-judge benchmarking.
rubric.low_score_criteria: Believes pure vector search is always sufficient for all queries or has no metrics for evaluating RAG outputs.

scoring.5: Authoritative research-grade mastery of hybrid retrieval, RRF math, two-stage re-ranking, and Ragas/TruLens evaluation frameworks.
scoring.3: Understands hybrid search and basic RAG metrics but lacks depth on re-ranking or RRF mechanics.
scoring.1: Only knows basic vector search embeddings.

title: Site Reliability: The Four Golden Signals and Incident Post-Mortems
content: What are Google SRE's Four Golden Signals? How do you establish Service Level Objectives (SLOs) and Error Budgets, and what makes a blameless post-mortem effective?
expected_answer: The Four Golden Signals are Latency (time to serve request), Traffic (demand/throughput), Errors (rate of failed requests), and Saturation (how full system resources are). A Service Level Objective (SLO) defines target reliability (e.g. 99.9% success rate), and the Error Budget is the remaining permitted unreliability (0.1%). If error budget is exhausted, feature deployments are paused to focus on reliability. A blameless post-mortem assumes engineers had good intentions and focuses on systemic safeguards, automated testing gaps, and architectural improvements rather than human error.

Explains SLOs and Error Budget governance
Defines principles of blameless post-mortem culture and systemic root causes

rubric.low_score_criteria: Confuses SLOs with SLAs or believes incidents should assign individual blame.
